name: MOTS-c
aliases: Mitochondrial open reading frame of the 12S rRNA-c
used_for: A 16-amino-acid peptide encoded in mitochondrial DNA, studied mostly in cells and rodents for insulin sensitivity, obesity, exercise capacity and aging. Online it is promoted for fat loss, energy and longevity. Human data is mostly measurements of natural MOTS-c blood levels; one early-stage injection trial is registered in China and has no results.

entries.text: Animal study only, not human data: a single 15 mg/kg dose of MOTS-c improved running time and distance in an acute exercise test in untrained mice.
A registered Phase 2a trial lists a fixed once-daily subcutaneous dose for 12 weeks versus placebo; the registry record does not state the dose amount, and no results are posted.
entries.population: Planned: adults 18 to 65 with prediabetes and overweight or obesity

internet_entries.text: A peptide protocol site (Path To Peptides, which discloses commission-earning links) says MOTS-c use is described as 5 to 10 mg per week, either as one weekly injection or split across two to three doses. The page carries affiliate links, so it is classed as vendor and not linked.
internet_entries.population: As described by the source, not a study population

internet_entries.text: A peptide directory site (PeptideProbe, which discloses affiliate links to telehealth services) says a typical MOTS-c dose is 5 to 10 mg subcutaneously, two to three times per week. The page carries affiliate links, so it is classed as vendor and not linked.
internet_entries.population: As described by the source, not a study population

administration_guidance.text: The registered phase 2a trial (NCT07505745) in adults with prediabetes and overweight/obesity uses subcutaneous injection once daily for 12 weeks, with a 4-week post-treatment safety follow-up. No results have been posted.
administration_guidance.label: research

administration_guidance.text: An educational site (PeptideFox) says MOTS-c is typically injected in the morning, ahead of exercise, and that a mixed vial is kept refrigerated at 2 to 8 C and used within 1 to 2 weeks.
administration_guidance.label: internet

administration_guidance.text: A clinic page (The Lamkin Clinic) says morning or pre-exercise timing is preferred for MOTS-c, given by subcutaneous injection and stored refrigerated after reconstitution.
administration_guidance.label: internet

administration_guidance.text: An educational site (PeptIQ, which carries referral links to clinics) says MOTS-c is taken fasted in the morning, 15 to 30 minutes before eating, that black coffee and plain tea are described as not breaking the fast, that morning use applies even for afternoon workouts, and that evening use is discouraged for missing the fasted window and possibly affecting sleep.
administration_guidance.label: internet

side_effects.text: An educational site (PeptideFox) says injection-site reactions such as burning, redness and lumps are the most frequent reports for MOTS-c, with mild fatigue and transient stomach discomfort also mentioned.
side_effects.label: internet

side_effects.text: A clinic page (The Lamkin Clinic) describes mild injection-site reactions and transient low blood sugar, mainly in people with insulin sensitivity or taking glucose-lowering medication, as reported with MOTS-c.
side_effects.label: internet

internet_claims.claim: A clinic's educational page says MOTS-c reduces abdominal fat, improves insulin sensitivity, boosts endurance and supports longevity, and mentions physician-supervised use while noting it is not FDA-approved.

A McGill University Office for Science and Society article says MOTS-c extended lifespan and improved metabolism in mice, but argues the hype among biohackers and influencers outruns the human evidence.

research.summary: Foundational paper (Cell Metab) identifying MOTS-c and testing it in cultured cells and mice, including mice on a high-fat diet. Some authors were later associated with a company developing related peptides.
research.finding: MOTS-c treatment prevented age-dependent and high-fat-diet-induced insulin resistance and diet-induced obesity in mice, acting mainly on skeletal muscle via AMPK. Mouse data only.

research.summary: Study (Nat Commun) of MOTS-c in young, middle-aged and old mice, plus a human measurement of MOTS-c after exercise. The authors disclosed ties to CohBar, Inc.
research.finding: MOTS-c improved physical performance in mice of all ages, and late-life intermittent treatment increased physical capacity and healthspan in mice. In humans, exercise raised the body's own MOTS-c in muscle and blood; people were not given the peptide.

research.summary: Rodent study (Physiol Rep) of MOTS-c levels after running and of a single MOTS-c dose before an exercise test.
research.finding: Running raised muscle MOTS-c in rodents, and one 15 mg/kg dose increased running time by about 12% and distance by about 15% in untrained mice. Single dose, animals only.

research.summary: Secondary analysis (Sci Rep) of a randomized exercise trial in 49 breast cancer survivors measuring natural MOTS-c in blood after 16 weeks of exercise. Authors disclosed a CohBar consulting tie.
research.finding: Blood MOTS-c rose after exercise in non-Hispanic White survivors but not in Hispanic survivors. No MOTS-c was administered, so it says nothing about injected MOTS-c.

research.summary: Registered Phase 2a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of daily subcutaneous MOTS-c for 12 weeks in about 120 adults with prediabetes and overweight or obesity, sponsored by Hudson Biotech. Listed as recruiting at one site in Shenzhen, China; the record states it is not an FDA-regulated drug study.
research.finding: No results exist yet (primary completion estimated 2027). It is the only registered MOTS-c injection trial found in ClinicalTrials.gov, and it is not a US pipeline trial.

research.summary: Registered Phase 1a/1b randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of CB4211, a drug related to MOTS-c (an analog, not MOTS-c itself), in 88 healthy non-obese adults and adults with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. It tested single doses, 7 days of daily injections under the skin, and 28 days of daily injections in the liver disease group. Completed April 2021 per the registry.
research.finding: The registry lists safety and injection-site reactions as the outcomes and posts no results. Any numbers reported elsewhere come from secondary sources, and the compound tested was an analog.

research.summary: FDA web page on bulk drug substances for compounding that may present significant safety risks (page dated 04/22/2026, fetched 2026-09-30).
research.finding: On the fetched page MOTS-c appears in the table of bulk drug substances nominated but later withdrawn, with FDA noting that compounded drugs containing MOTS-c may pose a significant risk of immunogenicity for certain routes of administration. The page does not describe an approved product.

dose.summary: No human dose of MOTS-c has been established. The only mouse dose in the research is 15 mg/kg in one exercise test, and a registered 12-week trial does not state its dose. Online sources describe 5 to 10 mg per injection or per week.

mechanism.summary: A small protein made by mitochondria, the cell's energy units. In mice it acts mainly on muscle through the energy sensor AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK). How it works in people is not established.

items.text: In cells and mice, MOTS-c acted mainly on skeletal muscle through AMPK and prevented age-related and high-fat-diet insulin resistance. Mouse and cell data only.
items.label: research

items.text: PeptideFox says MOTS-c activates AMPK, increases glucose uptake, promotes fat burning and builds new mitochondria.
items.label: internet

items.text: The Lamkin Clinic says MOTS-c activates AMPK and promotes mitochondria growth, cell cleanup, fat burning and glucose uptake.
items.label: internet

best_documented_effect.summary: Mouse studies show better insulin sensitivity, less diet-induced weight gain and better exercise capacity. In people, only natural MOTS-c levels have been measured, and no injection trial has reported results.

items.text: In mice, MOTS-c prevented diet-induced obesity and insulin resistance.
items.label: research

items.text: In mice of all ages MOTS-c improved physical performance, and exercise raised the body's own MOTS-c in people who were not given the peptide.
items.label: research

items.text: In breast cancer survivors in an exercise trial (49 people), natural blood MOTS-c rose after exercise in non-Hispanic White survivors but not in Hispanic survivors. No MOTS-c was given.
items.label: research

items.text: A McGill University article says MOTS-c extended lifespan and improved metabolism in mice. It says a small trial of daily injections for 30 days in 20 overweight people showed no weight loss but lower blood sugar and liver enzymes, and argues the hype outruns the human evidence.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptidesExplorer says the only human trial is of CB4211, a MOTS-c analog, in 20 obese patients, with liver enzyme ALT down 25%, AST down 17% and fasting glucose down 6%. It could not be traced to posted results.
items.label: internet

items.text: Revolution Health and Wellness, a clinic, says MOTS-c reduces abdominal fat, improves insulin sensitivity and boosts endurance, and notes it is not FDA-approved.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Online reports
side_effect_groups.summary: Online sources describe injection-site burning, redness and lumps, with mild tiredness and brief stomach upset. No controlled trial of MOTS-c has reported side effects.

items.text: PeptideFox says injection-site burning, redness, welts and lumps are the most frequent reports, with mild fatigue at first doses and transient stomach discomfort.
items.label: internet

items.text: The Lamkin Clinic describes mild injection-site reactions as reported with MOTS-c.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Low blood sugar
side_effect_groups.summary: MOTS-c improves insulin sensitivity in mice, and online sources warn of brief low blood sugar, mainly in people taking glucose-lowering medicine.

items.text: In mice, MOTS-c prevented insulin resistance. This is why a glucose-lowering effect is plausible, but it has not been measured with injected MOTS-c in people.
items.label: research

items.text: The Lamkin Clinic describes transient low blood sugar, mainly in people with insulin sensitivity or taking glucose-lowering medication.
items.label: internet

items.text: PeptidesExplorer warns that injecting fasted can occasionally cause mild low blood sugar symptoms.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: In trials
side_effect_groups.summary: The registered trials have no posted results. A McGill article says it knows of no adverse effects reported in people.

items.text: The registered Phase 1 trial of the related drug CB4211 lists adverse events and injection-site reactions as outcomes. No results are posted.
items.label: research

items.text: A McGill University article says it found no reported adverse effects in humans, and says MOTS-c did not block cell death, which lowers a cancer-promotion concern raised for a related peptide.
items.label: internet

side_effect_groups.title: Regulator warning
side_effect_groups.summary: The FDA lists MOTS-c among compounding substances that may carry significant safety risks and says it found no human exposure data.

items.text: FDA says compounded drugs containing MOTS-c may pose a significant risk of immune reactions (immunogenicity) for certain routes, and may have impurity and ingredient-characterization problems. It says it found no human exposure data and does not know whether MOTS-c would cause harm in people.
items.label: research
